claim: H1.8 depletion in Xenopus egg extracts increased condensin I (CAP-G) levels on mitotic chromatin.
source: Depletion of H1.8 increased the levels of both CAP-G and TOP2A on mitotic chromosomes, while adding back recombinant H1.8 rescued the phenotype (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 1D and western blot data in Figure 1E.

claim: H1.8 depletion in Xenopus egg extracts increased TOP2A levels on mitotic chromatin.
source: Depletion of H1.8 increased the levels of both CAP-G and TOP2A on mitotic chromosomes, while adding back recombinant H1.8 rescued the phenotype (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 1D and western blot data in Figure 1E.

claim: H1.8 depletion did not affect DNA replication in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: The dUTP quantitation also confirmed that H1.8 depletion did not affect DNA replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), as reported previously (Dasso et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by dUTP incorporation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citation to previous work.

claim: H1.8 depletion increased condensin II (CAP-G2) levels on mitotic chromatin.
source: Condensin II levels on chromosomes also showed similar increases in ΔH1 extracts by immunofluorescence and western blots on purified chromosomes, although peptides of condensin II-specific subunits were not detected by mass spectrometry (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1F-G and western blot data in Figure 1H.

claim: H1.8 preloading on nucleosome arrays reduces binding of condensin I to nucleosome arrays in vitro.
source: In the buffer condition where excess ATP was present over magnesium, preloading of H1.8 to the nucleosome array reduced binding of both wild-type and the ATP-binding-deficient Q-loop mutant of condensin I at physiological salt concentrations (50–150 mM NaCl) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: H1.8 preloading on nucleosome arrays reduces binding of condensin II to nucleosome arrays in vitro.
source: H1.8 also suppressed binding of condensin II and its Q-loop mutant to the nucleosome array (Figure 2C), though, as expected (Kong et al., 2020), condensin II showed higher affinity to the nucleosome array than condensin I.
evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2C and citation to previous work.

claim: H1.8 reduces binding of condensin I to mononucleosomes in vitro.
source: Supporting the direct competition model, H1.8 reduced binding of condensin I to mononucleosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: H1.8 reduces binding of TOP2A to nucleosome arrays at 120 mM NaCl in vitro.
source: As compared to condensins, TOP2A showed more stable binding to the nucleosome array, and H1.8 had no effect on TOP2A binding at low salt concentrations. However, H1.8 did reduce nucleosome array binding of recombinant Xenopus TOP2A at 120 mM NaCl (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: H1.8 depletion increases average chromosome length by approximately 50% in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: As reported previously (Maresca et al., 2005), average chromosome length increased by ~50% upon H1.8 depletion (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by chromosome length measurement data shown in Figure 3C-D and citation to previous work.

claim: Co-depletion of H1.8 and condensin I (CAP-G) results in chromosomes shorter than mock-depleted chromosomes.
source: Supporting our hypothesis, when condensin I was co-depleted (ΔH1ΔCAP-G), chromosomes became even shorter than chromosomes in mock-depleted extracts (ΔIgG) (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by chromosome length measurement data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Co-depletion of H1.8 and condensin II (CAP-D3) does not change chromosome length compared to H1.8 depletion alone.
source: In contrast, condensin II co-depletion (ΔH1ΔCAP-D3) did not change the chromosome length (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by chromosome length measurement data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Condensin II depletion alone does not affect chromosome length in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Chromosome length in condensin II-depleted extracts (ΔCAP-D3) was also indistinguishable from mock-depleted chromosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the negligible effect of condensin II depletion in the presence of normal levels of condensin I in Xenopus egg extracts (Shintomi and Hirano, 2011).
evidence: Supported by chromosome length measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and citation to previous work.

claim: When condensin I levels on chromatin in H1.8-depleted extracts are reduced to match control levels, chromosome lengths become equivalent to control.
source: When mitotic chromosomes were assembled in ∆H1.8 extracts that contain 40% (of ΔIgG) condensin I (CAP-G), condensin I level on these chromosomes was equivalent to that on chromosomes in control (∆IgG) extracts (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). Consistent with the hypothesis that H1.8 does not contribute to chromosome length regulation independently of condensin I, average chromosome length was essentially identical between these two conditions (ΔH1 40% CAP-G and ∆IgG; Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by condensin I immunofluorescence data in Figure 3E and chromosome length data in Figure 3F.

claim: Partial depletion of TOP2A in H1.8-depleted extracts leads to further increase in chromosome length, not a decrease.
source: Consistent with these observations, partial depletion of TOP2A in H1.8-depleted extracts also led to a further increase and not decrease in chromosome length (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E), suggesting that chromosome elongation in H1.8-depleted extracts was not caused by the increased level TOP2A on chromatin.
evidence: Supported by chromosome length data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: H1.8 depletion reduces the average loop size in mitotic chromosomes.
source: Although it is difficult to estimate the exact loop size from these plots, chromosomes from ΔH1 extracts showed a reproducible shift of the peak towards smaller genomic distances (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). This is consistent with a decrease in loop size due to increased condensin I accumulation on chromatin upon H1.8 depletion.
evidence: Supported by Hi-C derivative plot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Figure 4C.

claim: H1.8 depletion reduces the layer size from approximately 5 Mb to approximately 3.5 Mb.
source: For control chromosomes, the average amount of DNA in each layer of loops (layer size) was approximately 5 Mb, given the steep decay in contact probability observed for loci separated by more than 5 Mb for both replicates (Figure 4B and D). For H1.8-depleted chromosomes, we observed a smaller layer size of around 3.5 Mb (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C contact probability decay curve data shown in Figure 4B and derivative plot data in Figure 4D.

claim: The 1.5-fold reduction in layer size upon H1.8 depletion explains the observed 1.5-fold increase in chromosome length.
source: This 1.5-fold reduction of DNA content of each layer would explain the observed 1.5-fold increase in chromosome length (Figure 3D).
evidence: Inference based on Hi-C layer size data and chromosome length measurements.

claim: The number of loops per layer is approximately 40 in both control and H1.8-depleted extracts.
source: Further, we can derive the number of loops per layer by dividing the layer size by the loop size in the corresponding condition. In both control (ΔIgG) and H1.8-depleted extracts (ΔH1), the number of loops per layer was ~40.
evidence: Calculated from Hi-C data on layer size and loop size.

claim: The change in layer size upon H1.8 depletion is a result of decreased loop size, while the number of loops per layer is not affected.
source: This indicates that the change in the layer size upon H1.8 depletion is a result of decreased loop size, while the number of loops per layer is not affected.
evidence: Inference based on Hi-C data showing constant number of loops per layer despite changes in layer size.

claim: H1.8/condensin I co-depletion results in larger layer size than control extracts.
source: The layer size in H1.8/condensin I co-depleted extracts (ΔH1ΔCAP-G) was larger than those in control extracts (ΔIgG) (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C derivative plot data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Chromosomes in H1.8/condensin I co-depleted extracts are shorter than those in control extracts.
source: Further supporting the idea that the layer size anticorrelates with the chromosome length, chromosomes in ΔH1ΔCAP-G extracts were indeed shorter than those in control ∆IgG extracts (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: Supported by chromosome length data shown in Figure 3D and F.

claim: Condensin II co-depletion with H1.8 does not affect the layer size compared to H1.8 depletion alone.
source: Condensin II co-depletion (ΔH1ΔCAP-D3) did not affect the layer size (3.5 Mb) and also the chromosome length (Figures 4D, E, 3D).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C data in Figure 4D-E and chromosome length data in Figure 3D.

claim: Condensin II depletion alone does not affect the layer size.
source: Condensin II depletion alone (ΔCAP-D3) also did not affect the layer size, consistent with the observed lack of change in the chromosome length (Figure 4D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C data in Figure 4D-E and chromosome length data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3-H4 depletion increases chromatin-bound condensin I beyond that of H1.8 depletion.
source: As nucleosomes occupy a large majority of the genomic DNA (Lee et al., 2007; Chereji et al., 2019), even a partial histone depletion (ΔH3-H4) increased chromatin-bound condensin I beyond that of H1.8 depletion (ΔH1) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by condensin I immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and citations to previous work.

claim: H3-H4 depletion results in a much smaller layer size (around 500 kb) than H1.8 depletion.
source: Consequentially, the layer size in ∆H3-H4 extracts became much smaller (around 500 kb) than in ∆H1 extracts (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C derivative plot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Metaphase chromosomes in nocodazole-treated extracts cluster into tight ball-like structures.
source: In the presence of the microtubule depolymerizing drug nocodazole, metaphase chromosomes derived from each nucleus clustered to form tight ball-like structures (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ICRF-193 treatment completely blocks chromosome individualization when added at mitotic entry.
source: Indeed, when ICRF-193, the drug that inhibits topo II-dependent catenation/decatenation without leaving double-strand DNA breaks (Tanabe et al., 1991), was added to egg extracts at the mitotic entry, chromosome individualization was completely blocked, forming large chromosome clusters after extract dilution (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D, ICRF-50 min).
evidence: Supported by chromosome individualization assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D and citation to previous work.

claim: ICRF-193 treatment 2 minutes before extract dilution decreases efficiency of chromosome individualization.
source: Even when ICRF-193 was added to metaphase egg extracts after completion of metaphase chromatid formation, but 2 min before extract dilution (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, bottom), efficiency of chromosome individualization decreased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D, ICRF-2 min).
evidence: Supported by chromosome individualization assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Substantial interchromosomal topological catenations remain unresolved in metaphase and can be resolved by TOP2A during mechanical dispersion.
source: These results suggest that substantial interchromosomal topological catenations remain unresolved in metaphase and that these can be resolved by TOP2A during mechanical dispersion (via spindle or dilution).
evidence: Inference based on ICRF-193 treatment experiments showing persistent interchromosomal links.

claim: Condensin I depletion results in defective chromosome individualization.
source: Condensin I depletion (ΔCAP-G) resulted in defective chromosome individualization, suggesting that condensin I activity drives resolution of interchromosomal entanglements, and that condensin II is not sufficient to resolve these interchromosomal links in this background.
evidence: Supported by chromosome individualization assay data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Co-depletion of H1.8 and condensin I effectively rescues chromosome individualization without detectable CAP-G on chromatin.
source: Strikingly, co-depletion of H1.8 and condensin I (ΔH1ΔCAP-G) effectively rescued chromosome individualization without detectable CAP-G on chromatin (Figure 6A–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by chromosome individualization assay data shown in Figure 6B-C and condensin I immunofluorescence data in Figure 6D.

claim: The rescue of chromosome individualization in H1.8/condensin I co-depleted extracts requires condensin II.
source: This apparent bypass of condensin I requirement in chromosome individualization required condensin II as chromosome individualization failed in the triple-depleted extracts (ΔH1ΔCAP-G∆CAP-D3; Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by chromosome individualization assay data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Increased condensin II in H1.8/condensin I co-depleted extracts may replace the function of condensin I.
source: The increased condensin II in ΔH1ΔCAP-G extracts may replace the function of condensin I by condensin II in the absence of H1.8 (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by condensin II immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: H1.8 depletion results in more spread out chromosomes in nocodazole-treated extracts compared to control.
source: In contrast, individual chromosomes were more readily distinguished by DNA staining and spread to larger area in ΔH1 extracts, suggesting that the H1.8-mediated suppression of chromosome individualization is responsible for the chromosome clustering when spindle assembly is compromised (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Supported by surface area measurement data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: H1.8/condensin I co-depleted extracts show reduced chromosome clustering compared to control extracts in nocodazole-treated conditions.
source: However, H1.8 condensin I co-depleted extracts (ΔH1ΔCAP-G) showed reduced clustering compared to ∆IgG extracts, despite the shorter average chromosome length in ∆H1∆CAP-G extracts (Figure 3D,F), suggesting that chromosome spreading upon H1.8 depletion is not primarily driven by chromosome elongation but by chromosome hyper-individualization.
evidence: Supported by surface area measurement data shown in Figure 7E and chromosome length data in Figure 3D,F.

claim: Partial TOP2A depletion reduces chromosome spreading in H1.8/condensin I co-depleted extracts.
source: However, partial TOP2A depletion reduced chromosome spreading in H1.8/condensin I co-depleted (ΔH1ΔCAP-G) extracts, suggesting that suppression of both condensin I and topo II by H1.8 keeps egg extract chromosomes together during mitosis even in the absence of spindle microtubules.
evidence: Supported by surface area measurement data shown in Figure 7G-H.

claim: H1.8 limits chromatin levels of condensins and TOP2A to tune chromosome length and prevent hyper-individualization.
source: Here we demonstrated that H1.8 also plays a major role in regulation of long-range DNA interaction through controlling chromatin loading of condensins. Although condensins and topo II are activated in mitosis to drive chromosome segregation (Kimura et al., 1998; Hirano and Mitchison, 1991), we showed that their functionalities are antagonized by H1.8 to tune chromosome length and prevent hyper-individualization, which increases surface area (Figure 8, Table 1).
evidence: Summary statement supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript and citations to previous work.

claim: Condensin I binds weakly to mononucleosomes with linker DNA.
source: Condensin I binds weakly to mononucleosomes with linker DNA (Kong et al., 2020). We observed similar weak binding of condensin I to nucleosome arrays, and this binding was stimulated by ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and citation to previous work.

claim: ATP enhancement of condensin binding to nucleosome arrays is due to chelation of magnesium rather than ATP binding by condensin.
source: Since this enhancement was not seen when magnesium concentration was higher than the ATP concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), we hypothesized that ATP might have enhanced condensin binding to the nucleosome arrays by chelating magnesium, which is known to induce chromatin compaction (Finch and Klug, 1976; Eltsov et al., 2008). Indeed, both EDTA and ATP, which chelate magnesium, increased binding of the Q-loop mutant of condensin I to the nucleosome array (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D), suggesting that condensin binding to the nucleosome array is sensitive to high magnesium concentration and not due to ATP binding of condensin I.
evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C-D and citations to previous work.

claim: ATP does not stimulate condensin I binding to mononucleosomes.
source: In contrast, ATP did not stimulate condensin I binding to mononucleosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E), indicating that excess magnesium may limit condensin binding through compaction of the nucleosome array.
evidence: Supported by gel shift assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Condensin II shows higher affinity to nucleosome arrays than condensin I.
source: H1.8 also suppressed binding of condensin II and its Q-loop mutant to the nucleosome array (Figure 2C), though, as expected (Kong et al., 2020), condensin II showed higher affinity to the nucleosome array than condensin I.
evidence: Supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2C and citation to previous work.

claim: Recombinant human condensin I can functionally replace Xenopus condensin I in egg extracts.
source: As previously shown with human condensin I purified from HeLa cells (Kimura et al., 2001), our recombinant human condensin I, but not the ATP-binding defective Q-loop mutant (Hassler et al., 2019; Hopfner et al., 2000; Löwe et al., 2001; Kong et al., 2020), was able to rescue mitotic chromosome morphology defects caused by condensin I depletion in Xenopus extracts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), demonstrating that the recombinant human condensin I can also functionally replace Xenopus condensin I.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and citations to previous work.

claim: Recombinant X. laevis TOP2A is functional in Xenopus egg extracts and possesses ATP-dependent kinetoplast decatenation activity in vitro.
source: The recombinant X. laevis TOP2A used was also able to rescue chromatid formation in ΔTOP2A extracts and was able to perform ATP-dependent kinetoplast decatenation in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment and decatenation assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: Mitotic chromosomes in Xenopus egg extracts lack checkerboard patterns and topologically associating domains (TADs) characteristic of interphase chromosomes.
source: As seen in mitotic chromosomes in somatic cells (Naumova et al., 2013; Gibcus et al., 2018) and in early stages of mouse development (Du et al., 2017), all the Hi-C contact maps showed no checkerboard pattern commonly associated with interphase chromosome compartments and lacked any sign of topologically associating domains (TADs) (Szabo et al., 2019; Figure 4A; data available at GEO under accession no. GSE164434).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C contact map data shown in Figure 4A and citations to previous work.

claim: Condensin I depletion causes major changes in Hi-C maps reflecting severe morphological defects in mitotic chromosomes.
source: Condensin I depletion (∆CAP-G) caused a major change in the Hi-C map (Figure 4A), reflecting its severe morphological defects in mitotic chromosomes in Xenopus egg extracts (Hirano et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C contact map data shown in Figure 4A and citation to previous work.

claim: In Xenopus egg extracts, condensin I depletion affects interactions at longer distances (~10 Mb), whereas condensin II depletion does not cause recognizable changes in interactions at both long and short distances.
source: Unlike in DT40 cells, where depletion of condensin I and condensin II reduces interactions at shorter (<6 Mb) and longer (>6 Mb) distances, respectively (Gibcus et al., 2018), condensin I depletion affected interactions at longer distances (~10 Mb), whereas condensin II depletion (ΔCAP-D3) did not cause recognizable changes in interactions at both long and short distances (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C contact probability decay curve data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and citation to previous work.

claim: A second diagonal band indicative of helical organization in the chromosome axis was not seen in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: A second diagonal band, which is indicative of a strong helical organization in the chromosome axis (Gibcus et al., 2018), was not seen in Xenopus egg extracts (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), likely reflecting the minor contribution of condensin II in this system or perhaps due to a prolonged arrest in mitosis (Gibcus et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C contact map data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, and citation to previous work.

claim: H1.8 depletion causes a dramatic decrease in interactions at long genomic distances (1–10 Mb) in Hi-C analysis.
source: In H1.8-depleted extracts (∆H1), a dramatic decrease in interactions at long genomic distances (1–10 Mb) was observed (Figure 4A and B), as expected from the thinner chromosomes (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C contact map and contact probability decay curve data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The estimated loop size in control extracts is approximately 140 kb and in H1.8-depleted extracts is approximately 110 kb.
source: Derivative plots generated from Hi-C maps of dispersed chromosomes in diluted extracts (Figure 3A) showed a similar shift in the peak towards smaller genomic distances upon H1.8 depletion (Figure 4C). The derivative plots from these dispersed chromosomes showed a better-defined peak, allowing a coarse loop size estimate of ~140 kb in control (ΔIgG) extracts and ~110 kb in ΔH1 extracts using the previously reported derivative peak heuristic (Gassler et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by Hi-C derivative plot data shown in Figure 4C and citation to previous work.

claim: Condensin I plays the dominant role in the organization of loop layers in Xenopus egg extracts, not condensin II.
source: Taken together, these data support the hypothesis that H1.8 limits the condensin I level on chromatin and shortens chromosome lengths, allowing each condensin I to form a longer loop, and consequentially tuning the amount of DNA present in each layer. The data also suggest that unlike in chicken DT 40 cells condensin I and not condensin II plays the dominant role in the organization of loop layers (Gibcus et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference based on Hi-C data and comparison to previous work in DT40 cells.

claim: Global occupancy of nucleosomes and linker histones can affect DNA loop size and chromosome length through controlling the number of condensin molecules on the chromatin fiber.
source: Altogether these results suggest that global occupancy of nucleosomes and linker histones can affect DNA loop size and chromosome through controlling the number of condensin molecules on the chromatin fiber.
evidence: Summary inference based on H1.8 depletion and H3-H4 depletion experiments.

claim: Chromosomes from each nucleus in nocodazole-treated control extracts cluster into tight balls, but individualize normally upon extract dilution.
source: Although chromosomes from each nucleus tightly compact into a ball-like mass in nocodazole treated metaphase extracts (Figure 5B), they individualized normally by dispersion upon extract dilution (Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by surface area measurement data in Figure 5B-C and chromosome individualization assay data in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Interchromosomal contacts accumulated in the absence of spindles can be resolved by mechanical dispersion.
source: This suggests that the interchromosomal contacts accumulated in the absence of spindles can be resolved by mechanical dispersion.
evidence: Inference based on chromosome individualization assay data showing normal individualization after dilution in nocodazole-treated extracts.

claim: TOP2A inhibition by ICRF-193 almost completely blocks chromosome individualization in nocodazole-treated extracts.
source: TOP2A inhibition by treatment with ICRF-193 however almost completely blocked chromosome individualization in nocodazole-treated extracts (Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), confirming the accumulation of interchromosomal catenations in clustered chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by chromosome individualization assay data shown in Figure 5D-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Condensin I activity drives resolution of interchromosomal entanglements, and condensin II is not sufficient to resolve these interchromosomal links in the absence of condensin I.
source: Condensin I depletion (ΔCAP-G) resulted in defective chromosome individualization, suggesting that condensin I activity drives resolution of interchromosomal entanglements, and that condensin II is not sufficient to resolve these interchromosomal links in this background.
evidence: Inference based on chromosome individualization assay data showing defects upon condensin I depletion.

claim: H1.8-mediated suppression of condensin enrichment on chromatin limits chromosome individualization during mitosis.
source: These results demonstrate that H1.8-mediated suppression of condensin enrichment on chromatin limits chromosome individualization during mitosis.
evidence: Summary inference based on rescue of chromosome individualization in H1.8/condensin I co-depleted extracts.

claim: Chromosome individualization is sensitive to TOP2A levels on chromatin.
source: Upon reduction of TOP2A to 25%, the frequency of unindividualized chromosome clusters increased about threefold in ΔIgG background (Figure 7C). However, in the absence of H1.8, extracts with 25% levels of TOP2A were still able to support maximum level of chromosome individualization as chromosome-associated levels of TOP2A became equivalent to untreated control extracts (Figure 7C). These data suggest that chromosome individualization is sensitive to TOP2A levels on chromatin, and that H1.8 suppression of TOP2A plays a role in suppressing chromosome individualization.
evidence: Supported by chromosome individualization assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: H1.8 suppression of TOP2A plays a role in suppressing chromosome individualization.
source: These data suggest that chromosome individualization is sensitive to TOP2A levels on chromatin, and that H1.8 suppression of TOP2A plays a role in suppressing chromosome individualization.
evidence: Inference based on partial TOP2A depletion experiments showing effects on chromosome individualization.

claim: Chromosome spreading upon H1.8 depletion is not primarily driven by chromosome elongation but by chromosome hyper-individualization.
source: However, H1.8 condensin I co-depleted extracts (ΔH1ΔCAP-G) showed reduced clustering compared to ∆IgG extracts, despite the shorter average chromosome length in ∆H1∆CAP-G extracts (Figure 3D,F), suggesting that chromosome spreading upon H1.8 depletion is not primarily driven by chromosome elongation but by chromosome hyper-individualization.
evidence: Inference based on surface area measurements and chromosome length data.

claim: Suppression of both condensin I and topo II by H1.8 keeps egg extract chromosomes together during mitosis even in the absence of spindle microtubules.
source: However, partial TOP2A depletion reduced chromosome spreading in H1.8/condensin I co-depleted (ΔH1ΔCAP-G) extracts, suggesting that suppression of both condensin I and topo II by H1.8 keeps egg extract chromosomes together during mitosis even in the absence of spindle microtubules.
evidence: Inference based on surface area measurements in partial TOP2A depletion experiments.

claim: Regulating linker histone stoichiometry could serve as a rheostat to control chromosome length through tuning the condensin level on chromatin.
source: Since condensin I subunits are most abundant chromatin proteins whose levels were enhanced by H1.8 depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 1—source data 2), and chromosome lengths can be dictated by the amount of condensins in a manner independently of H1.8 (Figure 3F), we propose that regulating linker histone stoichiometry could serve as a rheostat to control chromosome length through tuning the condensin level on chromatin (Figure 8).
evidence: Inference based on mass spectrometry data and chromosome length experiments.

claim: Limiting chromosome length might be important for timely and synchronous segregation during rapid early embryonic cell divisions.
source: Since the larger cell size correlates with reduced mitotic checkpoint strength (Galli and Morgan, 2016; Minshull et al., 1994), limiting chromosome length might be important for their timely and synchronous segregation during the rapid early embryonic cell divisions.
evidence: Speculation based on known correlations between cell size and checkpoint strength.

claim: H1.8 may increase the loop size by simply reducing the number of condensin molecules on chromatin but may not necessarily inhibit the loop extrusion rate or processivity.
source: Since the length of chromosomes with similar condensin I levels is unaffected by the presence of H1.8 (Figure 3E,F), H1.8 may increase the loop size by simply reducing the number of condensin molecules on chromatin but may not necessarily inhibit the loop extrusion rate or processivity.
evidence: Inference based on chromosome length experiments with matched condensin I levels.

claim: The preference of topo II for binding linker DNA may explain the observation of well-spaced TOP2B binding peaks around well-spaced nucleosomes around CTCF-binding sites.
source: The preference of topo II for binding linker DNA may also explain the observation of well-spaced TOP2B binding peaks around the well-spaced nucleosomes around the CTCF- binding sites (Canela et al., 2017; Canela et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference based on in vitro binding data and citations to previous work.

claim: TOP2A plays a structural role in axial compaction of mitotic chromosomes through its C-terminal chromatin-binding domain.
source: These data support the proposed structural role for TOP2A in axial compaction of mitotic chromosomes through its C-terminal chromatin-binding domain (Nielsen et al., 2020; Shintomi and Hirano, 2021; Lane et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference based on TOP2A depletion experiments and citations to previous work.

claim: Condensins and topo II combine to resolve extensive and persistent interchromosomal topological entanglement during mitotic compaction in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Our data also suggest that condensins and topo II combine to resolve extensive and persistent interchromosomal topological entanglement during mitotic compaction in Xenopus egg extracts (Figure 5), but these activities are counterbalanced by H1.8.
evidence: Inference based on chromosome individualization assay data.

claim: In HeLa cells, partial H1 eviction in prophase seems to be required for complete decatenation along chromosome arms.
source: In HeLa cells, somatic variants of H1 are phosphorylated and evicted along the inter-chromatid axis. This partial H1 eviction in prophase seems to be required for complete decatenation along the chromosome arms (Krishnan et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous work on H1 eviction in HeLa cells.

claim: Local enrichment of condensins (particularly condensin II) upon H1 eviction may play a role in sister chromatid decatenation.
source: This suggests that local enrichment of condensins (particularly condensin II) upon H1 eviction may play a role in sister chromatid decatenation.
evidence: Inference based on H1 eviction data in HeLa cells.

claim: H1.8 binding to nucleosomes is enhanced upon transition from interphase to M phase in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: In contrast, H1.8 binding to nucleosomes is enhanced upon transition from interphase to M phase in Xenopus egg extracts (Arimura et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to previous work on H1.8 binding dynamics.

claim: Keeping chromosomes at metaphase plate might be important for maintaining robust bipolar spindle in oocytes.
source: Since spindle assembly in oocytes relies on chromatin-induced microtubule nucleation (Heald et al., 1996), keeping chromosomes at metaphase plate might be important for maintaining robust bipolar spindle.
evidence: Speculation based on known mechanism of spindle assembly in oocytes.

claim: Microtubule-independent chromosome clustering may be particularly important for large oocyte and early embryonic cells to facilitate bipolar spindle assembly.
source: As we showed that H1.8 is important for chromosome clustering when spindle assembly is inhibited (Figure 7), this microtubule-independent chromosome clustering may be particularly important for the large oocyte and early embryonic cells since it would be difficult to assemble a bipolar spindle onto all the chromosomes once they disperse into the large space of the cytoplasm.
evidence: Speculation based on surface area measurement data and cell size considerations.

claim: Clustering chromosomes through incomplete individualization may avoid generation of chromosomes that do not associate with the spindle.
source: Clustering chromosomes through incomplete individualization may also avoid generation of chromosomes that do not associate with the spindle. Such a mechanism would facilitate effective kinetochore attachment during early embryonic cell divisions when the spindle checkpoint cannot be activated by unattached chromosomes (Mara et al., 2019; Gerhart et al., 1984; Hara et al., 1980).
evidence: Speculation based on known properties of early embryonic cell divisions.

claim: Paternal and maternal chromosomes cluster at the interface of two pronuclei prior to the first zygotic mitosis after fertilization to facilitate rapid and efficient kinetochore microtubule attachment in human and bovine embryos.
source: Indeed, it was recently shown that paternal and maternal chromosomes cluster at the interface of two pronuclei prior to the first zygotic mitosis after fertilization to facilitate rapid and efficient kinetochore microtubule attachment in human and bovine embryos (Cavazza et al., 2021).
evidence: Citation to recent work on chromosome clustering in human and bovine embryos.

claim: Resolution of DNA linkages in oocyte chromosomes may be prevented by H1.8-mediated suppression of condensin and TOP2A.
source: During long natural arrest at meiotic metaphase II, these centromeres undergo cohesion fatigue, where centromeres prematurely separate. However, proper segregation may still be accomplished due to apparent inter-chromatids DNA linkages (Gruhn et al., 2019). Resolution of these DNA linkages may be prevented by H1.8-mediated suppression of condensin and TOP2A.
evidence: Speculation based on known cohesion fatigue phenomenon and H1.8 function.

claim: H1.8 may play a condensin and TOP2A-independent role in regulating chromosome individualization.
source: However, our data do not eliminate the possibility that H1.8 plays a condensin and TOP2A-independent role in regulating chromosome individualization.
evidence: Acknowledgment of alternative possibilities not ruled out by the data.

claim: Regulation of Ki-67 may be a candidate for H1-mediated regulation of chromosome individualization.
source: Regulation of Ki-67, which coats the surface of chromosomes, may be a good candidate of H1-mediated regulation (White et al., 2016; Gibson et al., 2019; Cuylen et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation based on known properties of Ki-67 and citations to previous work.

claim: Changing the H1 stoichiometry on chromatin by changing the amount, subtype, and/or affinity of H1 affects the length and individualization of chromosomes through regulating the levels of condensins and topo II.
source: We expect that changing the H1 stoichiometry on chromatin by changing the amount, subtype, and/or affinity (e.g., through post-translational modifications) of H1 affects the length and individualization of chromosomes through regulating the levels of condensins and topo II.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results with H1.8.

claim: Somatic histone H1 fails to rescue chromosome elongation phenotype of H1.8 depletion because importin β sequesters somatic H1 and suppresses its binding to mitotic chromosomes.
source: In Xenopus egg extracts, somatic histone H1 fails to rescue chromosome elongation phenotype of H1.8 depletion since highly abundant importin β sequesters the somatic H1 and suppresses its binding to mitotic chromosomes (Freedman and Heald, 2010).
evidence: Citation to previous work on somatic H1 behavior in Xenopus egg extracts.

claim: H1.8 suppresses chromosome fragmentation mediated by microtubule-dependent force during sperm male pronucleus reorganization.
source: It has been shown that the sperm male pronucleus dynamically interacts with microtubules during its dramatic nuclear reorganization upon exposure to the egg cytoplasm (Xue et al., 2013), during which H1.8 suppresses chromosome fragmentation mediated by microtubule-dependent force (Xiao et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to previous work on H1.8 function during fertilization.

claim: H1.8 may be tuned to provide chromatin with physical strength of bulk chromatin rather than facilitating chromosome individualization during the unique fertilization process.
source: Thus, it is possible that H1.8 is tuned to provide chromatin with physical strength of bulk chromatin rather than facilitating chromosome individualization during the unique fertilization process.
evidence: Speculation based on known H1.8 functions during fertilization.

claim: Linker histones serve important interphase roles through regulation of transcription.
source: Linker histones also serve important interphase roles through regulation of transcription (Izzo et al., 2008), and the epigenetic landscape of the chromatin determines the linker histone variant on chromatin (Th'ng et al., 2005; Parseghian et al., 2001; Izzo et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to previous work on linker histone functions in interphase.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that linker histones also inhibit condensin II and cohesin binding in interphase.
source: Since H1.8 competitively inhibits condensin binding in mitosis, it is tempting to speculate that linker histones also inhibit condensin II and cohesin binding in interphase.
evidence: Speculation based on H1.8 function in mitosis.

claim: Local and global regulation of chromatin structure and function can be regulated by controlling differential expression of linker histone H1 variants and their modifications not just through promoting inter-nucleosomal interactions but also by controlling accessibility of SMC proteins and topo II.
source: We suggest that local and global regulation of chromatin structure and function can be regulated by controlling differential expression of linker histone H1 variants and their modifications not just through promoting inter-nucleosomal interactions but also by controlling accessibility of SMC proteins and topo II.
evidence: Summary inference based on all experimental results.

claim: The linker histone can suppress chromosome individualization and long-range DNA folding.
source: Thus, the linker histone H1, which can promote local chromatin compaction through promoting nucleosome-nucleosome interaction, can also suppress chromosome individualization and long-range DNA folding.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental results.

claim: DNA loop extrusion by condensins and decatenation by DNA topoisomerase II are thought to drive mitotic chromosome compaction and individualization.
source: DNA loop extrusion by condensins and decatenation by DNA topoisomerase II (topo II) are thought to drive mitotic chromosome compaction and individualization.
evidence: Statement of prevailing model in the field.

claim: H1.8 inhibits binding of condensins and topo II to nucleosome arrays in vitro.
source: In vitro chromatin reconstitution experiments demonstrate that H1.8 inhibits binding of condensins and topo II to nucleosome arrays.
evidence: Summary of in vitro binding assay results.

claim: H1.8 depletion makes chromosomes thinner and longer through shortening the average loop size and reducing the DNA amount in each layer of mitotic loops.
source: Chromosome morphology and Hi-C analyses suggest that H1.8 depletion makes chromosomes thinner and longer through shortening the average loop size and reducing the DNA amount in each layer of mitotic loops.
evidence: Summary of chromosome morphology and Hi-C analysis results.

claim: Excess loading of condensins and topo II to chromosomes by H1.8 depletion causes hyper-chromosome individualization and dispersion.
source: Furthermore, excess loading of condensins and topo II to chromosomes by H1.8 depletion causes hyper-chromosome individualization and dispersion.
evidence: Summary of chromosome individualization assay results.

claim: Condensins and topo II are essential for chromosome individualization, but their functions are tuned by the linker histone to keep chromosomes together until anaphase.
source: We propose that condensins and topo II are essential for chromosome individualization, but their functions are tuned by the linker histone to keep chromosomes together until anaphase.
evidence: Summary proposal based on all experimental results.
